extracted.intended_audience: English readers/travelers interested in early-19th-century Buenos Ayres customs and civic regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive account of social, religious, funerary, policing, and military customs and local regulations observed in Buenos Ayres in the 1820s. Focuses on customary obligations, civic rules, and punitive practices affecting residents and strangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy Thursday: visit seven churches
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule of Catholic creed enjoins them to visit seven churches on this day; the governor and his aides-de-camp likewise go to seven churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stops are brief (just time enough to kneel and utter a short prayer). This is a widely observed obligation among the populace during Holy Thursday processions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kneel and uncover for Holy Ghost procession
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Holy Ghost proceeds through the streets, a bell warns passengers of its approach, and all within view must be uncovered and, when near the carriage, kneel; equestrians descend from their horses and kneel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At guardhouses the guards turn out and drums are beaten. The text notes that 'strangers are not now obliged to kneel' (a later restraint on enforcement), though common respect still leads many to comply. There are anecdotes of enforcement excesses (a soldier once knocked an Englishman down for not kneeling in time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral-room presentation customs
rubrics_metrics.description: The room in which a corpse is deposited is lighted; large candles are placed round the coffin; wainscoting, tables, etc., are covered with white furniture, crosses, &c.; windows are often thrown open for passengers to view the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coffin lids are sometimes taken off and corpses displayed with hands folded and a small cross. These practices function as public reminders of mortality and are described as customary features of funerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interment timing in warm climate (24 hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceased persons are interred twenty-four hours after their decease; a necessary precaution in a warm climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because churchyards were crowded, corpses were moved to a New Burial-Ground; moving bodies after burial caused scenes of confusion and distress when relatives recognized remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protestant burial-ground procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Protestants were allotted a separate burial ground (opened circa 1821) with a small chapel; the service is read by some of the parties present and the interment is conducted following English/Protestant forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Protestant community funded the ground (expense cited as 4800 dollars). The author notes numbers buried and that Buenos Ayreans sometimes attended Protestant funerals out of curiosity and approval of deeper graves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masses for repose: printed invitations and ceremonial features
rubrics_metrics.description: Masses for the repose of the soul are performed at various churches according to relatives' wishes; printed notices invite friends and 'any one is at liberty to attend.' The ceremony lasts from one to two hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremonial elements include an imitation coffin near the altar surrounded by lights; for military or public men the sword and hat are placed on the coffin and a company of soldiers fire a volley at the church door; near the end candles are distributed to the male part of the congregation and then extinguished; priests and friars receive and return obeisances. Relations often adjourn afterwards to a repast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police organisation: alcalde and night-patrol
rubrics_metrics.description: To every barrier or parish an alcalde (sitting magistrate) is appointed, who takes cognizance of offences and disputes in his jurisdiction and superintends the night-patrol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Night patrols are armed with muskets and bayonets and proceed through the streets at intervals, visiting public houses. The alcaldes handle local offences and supervise these patrol duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Night-watch obligation: every male liable to serve or hire a substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: Every male is liable to be called out to act as watchman for the night; he must attend or provide a substitute, which costs six reals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The obligation is frequent enough that strangers find it a tax. A messenger delivering the summons for the nightly patrol commonly carries a sword as his staff of office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on wearing knives
rubrics_metrics.description: A law prohibiting the wearing of knives was enacted (cited as reducing the frequency of fatal stabbings among the lower orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law decreased the crime somewhat, but the author argues that until 'certain and speedy punishment' follows, the practice may persist. The prohibition is presented as a partial reform to curb violent quarrels that otherwise often end in murder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal punishments: shooting for death sentences; public whipping and irons for lesser penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital punishment is carried out by shooting. Public whipping is used (offender placed on a horse or mule with back bared) and prisoners sentenced to imprisonment are made to work in the streets heavily ironed; sailors are punished by the stocks and forced labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author comments on perceived appropriateness (some think hanging more suitable for murder). Public whippings are described as disgusting spectacles; convict labour in irons is routine for those imprisoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgery penalties and historical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The first execution in this country for forgery occurred in February 1825 (shot at the Retiro). By the old Spanish law a person convicted of forgery was condemned to lose his hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier commuted punishments included exposure in the Plaza, imprisonment for years, and banishment for life. The case of Marcelo Valdivia is given as an example, including earlier commutations and later recidivism leading to execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passport requirement to leave town or country
rubrics_metrics.description: To leave Buenos Ayres, even for a neighbouring town, passports must be obtained; they cost two dollars to quit the country and four reals for any neighbouring town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreigners are sometimes surprised that such travel formalities are required, with anecdotes of visiting officers requesting English passports from arrivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army composition, recruitment, dress, and disciplinary practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The standing army consists of 2,500–3,000 men in six regiments (three infantry, three cavalry) with two regiments of Civicas (militia). Recruits are not immediately clothed in uniform and the army 'takes every one they can.' Flogging is used to maintain discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Troops have improved in appearance and discipline but lack many European manoeuvres; artillery corps and regimental bands make notable contributions. Officers often retain fine uniforms while recruits remain poorly clothed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military funeral rites (sword/hat and volley)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a military or public man, the sword and hat are placed on the coffin and a company of soldiers fire a volley at the church door during the mass for the repose of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a ceremonial element distinguishing military funerals from regular masses; it typically accompanies the imitation coffin and the extended mass ceremony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public display of bodies for recognition and burial fundraising
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies of persons who had been stabbed were sometimes exposed in the Plaza to be recognized by relatives, with a saucer placed at their side to collect money to pay the expenses of burying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This public display practice arose from poverty and lack of organized burial funds; it could cause distress and imprecations when relatives recognized bodies thought lost.
